zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference: the supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida (CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). It was consulted after independent scan reading. The scan governs spelling, allographs, typography and lineation; the revised transcription and English notes are this review's own. Scan source: BnF Gallica / Bibliothèque nationale de France.

runs.text: dà preſencialmente por palaura, ou por eſcrito

lines.note: Continues the accusation entry at the end of f253: the accusation is made in person, orally or in writing. The grave in dà is visible; no final stop is supplied where the row ends without one.

runs.text: Vestido, ou habito que os Bonzos

lines.note: Giqitot denotes the monks' outer garment, identifiable as jikitotsu. The first t is abraded, leaving its bar and lower turn; Giqitot is preferred over OCR Giqicot, supported by the garment gloss and the supplied NINJAL headword, but that damaged letter remains a nonblocking uncertainty. Bonzos is Portuguese vocabulary, not a Japanese typeface term.
Completes the garment definition: the monks wear it over their other clothing. The long s in veſtem belongs to the italic Portuguese continuation, not to a new entry.

runs.text: Nouas de couſas que hum vio.

lines.note: Giqixet is firsthand news: reports of things someone personally saw. The checked final t and the printed vio are retained rather than expanded or modernized.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Pratica que hum faz preſencialmen

lines.note: Adds the sense of a discourse delivered personally. The final group reads men, not OCR mem, and continues as te on the next physical row; there is no visible terminal hyphen.
Completes preſencialmente and specifies that the speaker delivers the discourse himself. The entire short row belongs to the preceding additional sense.
Giqixi is one's own child; Giqino co is the explanatory Japanese phrase. The second letter group in Giqino is qi, not the OCR tqi sequence, and matches the direct/own sense of the entry.

Giqixo concerns a personally written or signed letter; Giqini caqu means to write directly/oneself. The scan supports Giqini, not Giqinri, and the final article is o, agreeing with ſinal on the following row.

runs.text: proprio ſinal, ou de ſua propria mão.

lines.note: The letter bears the writer's own signature or is in his own hand. The two alternatives explain the preceding Giqixo rather than introducing separate entries.
Giqua is earthly fire, contrasted with Tenqua, heavenly fire, in the example. The first half of the Portuguese translation ends with ceo and continues below.
Completes the contrast between fire from heaven and fire from the earth. The ampersand and final stop are both retained on this physical row.
Giri here means proceeds or revenues from land. The following example begins Giriuo muſa-boru, greedy extraction of those revenues; the printed hyphen after muſa is retained.

runs.text: Tirar cõ inuẽções ou injustamente prouei

lines.note: Completes muſaboru and begins the explanation of taking revenues by contrivances or unjustly. Both nasal abbreviations in cõ and inuẽções are retained; prouei continues onto the next row without a printed hyphen.
Completes proueito and restates it as income from lands. This is the continuation of the example under Giri, not an independent definition.
Giron is a dispute about land, explained by Chiuo ronzuru. The Portuguese alternates altercation with demanda, which begins as de at the right edge without a hyphen.
Completes demanda and locates the dispute in land matters. The printed a cerca is two words and is not silently modernized to acerca.
Giſan means bringing something along, with Motte mairu as its Japanese explanation. The Portuguese definition uses both levar and trazer; al- begins the next row's algũa.
Completes bringing some object with oneself and gives humble verbal alternatives. The printed tçu starts tçucamatçuru on the next row, without an added hyphen; l remains the Latin alternative marker.
Completes tçucamatçuru, then introduces the sentence about bringing the sake from the speaker's side. Both the continuation and the new Japanese example stay on the same physical row.

runs.text: Quãto ao vinho eu o leuarei de cà.

lines.note: Completes the humble prospective expression: as for the wine, I shall bring it from here. The central s is visibly short between the two caroned vowels in mǒsǒzu; the tilde in Quãto and grave in cà are retained.
Giſui combines earth and water, explicitly glossed by Tçuchi and mizzu. The historical spelling agoa is preserved in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de ſoar quando ſe

lines.note: Gitagitato is marked as an adverb describing a sound. Its environment is supplied in the next row, so the definition should not be detached from that continuation.
The sound occurs when one steps on wet ground, suggesting a squelching or splashing noise. The long s in piſa and the abbreviation &c. are retained.

runs.text: Sujeito, ou fundamento de qualquer cou

lines.note: Gitai denotes a subject or underlying basis of something. Sujeito here belongs with fundamento, not necessarily a person; cou continues as ſa below without a hyphen.
Completes couſa and adds the usage naturally, qualified by the Latin Aliquando, sometimes. The mixed-language wording is retained as printed rather than recast as modern Portuguese.

runs.text: O ſenhor, ou gouernador da terra.

lines.note: Gitô is the lord or governor of a territory. The headword's mark is a circumflex, unlike the carons on several neighboring entries, and is preserved as ô.

runs.text: ¶ Item, O ſenhor dalgum campo, ou chão,

lines.note: Adds the narrower sense of the owner or lord of a field or plot. The comma indicates that the description continues into the following row.

runs.text: em que hum mora, ou tem caſas.

lines.note: Completes the landholder sense with land on which someone resides or has houses. The Portuguese hum and the long s in caſas remain diplomatic spellings.

Giuari means dividing land into plots; Yaxiqiuo varu supplies the Japanese explanation. The i, marker belongs to that explanation and does not make these ordinary Japanese words embedded Portuguese terms.

runs.text: ou campo pera fazer caſas. ¶ Item, Pa-

lines.note: The plots are divided for house building. A second sense begins Pa-pel, introducing a plan or drawing of the division; the visible terminal hyphen is retained.

runs.text: pel, ou taboa onde eſtà a repartição do chão

lines.note: Completes Papel and describes the paper or board on which the subdivision is shown. The grave in eſtà is visible and the line continues without final punctuation.
Completes the description of a plan for placing houses. This remains Giuari's second sense, not a separate construction term.
Giuǒ is identified only as a medicinal herb by this printed gloss. The caron and the nasal abbreviation in Hũa are retained; a botanical species is not inserted into the transcription.
Giuǒxen names a kind of Japanese confection, described as alfeloas. The shared beginning with the preceding herb does not justify adding an ingredient or medicinal claim absent from this entry.

Gixei concerns governing the realm, with Youo voſamuru as its Japanese paraphrase. The initial G has a worn inner bar but retains the form seen in neighboring G initials; the gloss and supplied NINJAL Gixei corroborate the correction of OCR Cixei. The Portuguese ad- continues below.
Completes administrar o imperio, administration of the realm. The physical division after ad- is retained rather than merging the rows.

runs.text: Certo lanço, ou mão de jo

lines.note: Gixeqi, alternatively gi ixi, introduces a position or turn in the board game Go. The printed separation gi ixi is preserved, and jo continues as go on the next row without a hyphen.

runs.text: em q̃ dambas as partes ficão ẽ algũ

lines.note: Completes jogo and explains a Go position in which both sides remain in a certain area. The damaged but discernible ficão replaces OCR fuão; dambas and both nasal abbreviations remain unchanged. Go is an embedded Japanese game name and is set in Roman in this otherwise italic explanation.

runs.text: certo lugar ſem ganhar, nem perder.

lines.note: Completes the Go definition: neither side gains nor loses in that position. This balanced result supplies the meaning of the preceding Gixeqi/gi ixi rather than a general statement about all Go games.

runs.text: Foro do chão em que hum mora, ou dal-

lines.note: Gixi here is the due or rent for land on which one lives, or for a field. The final dal- joins gum below, and the fiscal sense is distinct from the following verbal headword.
Completes dalgum campo and gives Gixiuo naſu as paying the land due. The translation begins Pagar and is completed by the short next row.
Completes Pagar eſte foro, paying this land rent or due. It belongs to the example under the first Gixi entry.

The verbal Gixi entry means curing illness, with the printed principal parts ſuru, ita. These are preserved rather than repaired to a regularized paradigm; Ya- begins yamai, illness, in the example below.
Completes Yamaiuo giſuru, to cure an illness, and begins the additional sense of governing lands. The medical and governing senses share the printed verbal entry.
Completes the governing sense with kingdoms and gives Cuniuo giſuru, to govern a country. The two physical rows together supply the full administrative example.
Gixin is an earthquake, paraphrased by Chi furǔ, earth shaking. The final vowel of furǔ carries a caron; ter begins terremoto below without a visible hyphen.
Completes terremoto and gives the example Gixinga ſuru, an earthquake occurs. Its Portuguese explanation continues with terra on the final row.
Completes Tremer a terra, the earth shaking. The second vowel is e in the scan, correcting OCR tarra; this short line is body text above the bottom rule, not furniture.
Gixu is a landowner, explained by Gino nuxi. The Portuguese introduces examples of kinds of land and ends with the printed co- of como.
Completes como and lists low-lying agricultural land, a plot, or a field. These are examples under Gixu, not separate headwords.
Giyacu is an office or oversight concerning lands. The italic noun reads ſuperintendencia, with u after the long s, correcting OCR ſaperintendencia.
Completes the scope of the office: fields or lands. The entire short row is the Portuguese continuation under Giyacu.

runs.text: Aſomar, que he a primeira eſpecie de

lines.note: Gizan is addition, described as the first kind of reckoning. The scan reads eſpecie, not OCR eſperie; the historical Aſomar is retained rather than changed to modern somar.

Completes the account of addition and gives Gizanuo voqu, to set up an addition. No stop is inserted after voqu where none is secure; Caqe- starts the separate multiplication term on the same physical row.
Completes Caqezan, multiplication, and introduces Fiqizan, subtraction. The Portuguese Di- continues as minuir below; neither term is confused with the first addition entry.
Completes diminuir for subtraction and gives Faſſan as division. The printed double long s is retained in the Japanese term.

runs.text: Certo Idolo de vulto inferior a Fotoque.

lines.note: Gizǒ names an image/deity characterized by the historical dictionary as lower than Fotoque. That hierarchy is the source's description, not a new assertion; Fotoque is an embedded Japanese term, retained within the italic span and flagged for whole-word typeface review. The headword has a caron.

runs.text: Palaura, ou mandado: não ſe vſa ſem

lines.note: This Giǒ means a word or command and is said not to occur without an accompanying particle. The qualification continues on the next row and is essential to the usage statement.
Completes the restriction: Go or another particle accompanies Giǒ. Go is embedded metalinguistic material within the Portuguese explanation; Gogiǒde begins a separate Japanese example.

Completes the example meaning it is the lord's command and begins Côgiǒ, an oral message. Enlargement shows a circumflex but no secure hyphen after Cô before the right rule, so the OCR hyphen is removed rather than supplied by the word division.
Completes Côgiǒ and defines a message sent by word of mouth. The close printed ſemãda and both nasal abbreviations are retained, rather than silently expanding se manda.

This separate Giǒ entry is illustrated by Giǒni iru or nhǔgiǒ ſuru. The following explanation describes entering a terminal religious practice; the carons and the alternative marker l are kept exactly, and Me- begins Meterſe below.

runs.text: terſe viuo de baixo da terra, ou no fogo, ou

lines.note: Completes Meterſe and records the source's examples of entering earth or fire while alive. This is a historical dictionary gloss, not a prescription, and the third alternative continues below.

runs.text: na agoa afogandoſe, & morrendo como fazẽ

lines.note: Adds water, drowning, and dying, in the historical explanation of the preceding expression. The nasal abbreviation fazẽ and the reflexive afogandoſe are retained without modernizing the spelling.

Completes the historical statement by attributing those practices to some non-Christian monks. The qualifier algũs limits the claim; Bonzos is Portuguese terminology rather than a Japanese Roman-type insertion.
This homonymous Giǒ means determining or fixing, explained by Sadamuru. The example begins Giǒde and continues with gozaru on the next row.
Completes the expression for something certain or established. The explanation keeps both certa and aueriguada, distinguishing this Giǒ from the earlier command and religious senses.

runs.text: Palaura que ſe ajunta a numero de va-

lines.note: This Giǒ is a word combined with numbers for various things. The row ends va- of varias; the following restriction and examples clarify that this is a counting element.

runs.text: rias couſas, mas não ſe vſa por ſi ſoo ſe não,

lines.note: Completes varias and says the counting word is not used by itself but in combinations. Enlargement shows two o letters in ſoo, correcting the omitted vowel; I- starts Ichigiô below.

Completes Ichigiô and lists nigiô, iccagiô and nicagiô as counting combinations. Enlarged inspection shows the dotted i and repeated c of iccagiô; the c in nicagiô is abraded into horizontal remnants, not a secure z. The coherent one/two combinations support these selected readings, while the worn c groups remain a nonblocking caveat. All four printed vowel marks are circumflexes, although the headword uses a caron.
Gio means woman, with Vonna as the Japanese explanation. The following example begins irogonomi across the printed hyphen; this short-vowel headword is not normalized to neighboring Giǒ.
Completes Gio irogonomiuo ſuru, glossed as going about with women. The example concerns amorous pursuit, while the transcription retains the source's brief wording.
Giǒban is an assigned or fixed watch, paraphrased by Sadamatta ban. The Portuguese determi continues as nada without a terminal hyphen.

Completes determinada and gives an injunction not to neglect the assigned watch. The example prints Giobanuo without a secure vowel mark; faint isolated damage above o is insufficient to impose the headword's caron.
Translates the injunction as do not fail in your watch. The ligature ß in voßa is retained, not replaced by a modern ss sequence.
Giǒbu denotes something strong, with Tçuyoi coto as its Japanese explanation. The forthcoming example extends that quality to a strong man.

The Japanese example says that the strong man takes a sharp sword; the source's Portuguese begins the strong and valiant. The second noun is riqen, not a modernized spelling, and va continues below without a hyphen.
Completes valente and translates possession or taking of a sword. The alternative verbs tem and toma are both retained.
Giǒbuna is the attributive form meaning strong, illustrated with iye, a house. Both occurrences retain the caron.
Translates the example as a strong house, then adds the sense of a strong and steadfast man. The ampersand anticipates the adjective on the next row.
Completes Homem forte, & constante, emphasizing steadfastness as well as strength. The printed short s in constante is retained rather than mechanically converted to long s.
Giǒbuni is explicitly the adverb strongly. Xirouo starts an example about holding a fortress; it is ordinary Japanese example text rather than an embedded Portuguese typeface term.
Completes holding the fortress firmly. The T of Ter belongs to the italic Portuguese word, correcting the OCR font break that isolated it as Roman Japanese; the printed forte- continues below.
Completes fortemente and the idiom about maintaining a firm hold on the fortress. This row is solely the Portuguese continuation.

Giǒbutai is a permanent stage, contrasted with a temporary performance location. The Japanese paraphrase remains Ma vtena as printed; the Portuguese reads ſempre ha, not OCR ſempreba, with a separate h ascender and word gap.

runs.text: ou lugar determinado pera fazer os autos.

lines.note: Adds a designated place for performing plays. Autos is theatrical in this context, and pera remains the printed historical form.

Giochǔ denotes a respectable married woman in this gloss. The final u and its caron are poorly inked; the small angled trace above the vowel, together with the supplied NINJAL Giochǔ, supports the selected accented reading, retained as a nonblocking damaged-mark uncertainty.

runs.text: Cheiro, ou perfume que ſempre arde

lines.note: Giǒcǒ denotes incense or fragrance kept burning continually. Both vowels carry carons, although the second is faint; the objects before which it burns are supplied on the next row.

Completes the description of incense burning before Camis or Fotoques. These Japanese religious terms occur inside the Portuguese explanation and are flagged for whole-word typeface review; the existing italic span and the nasal abbreviation diãte are retained.

Giocuacu means evil or sin, paraphrased by Nigoru acu. The partially worn o in Nigoru is retained in agreement with the visible outline and the Japanese sense of defilement; peca- begins pecado below.
Completes pecado and gives the example of a world affected by evil. The printed in- begins the Portuguese word continued on the next row.
Completes inficionado de maldades, a world infected or tainted with evil. The ascender read by OCR as a separate l is the worn d of ficionado; no word boundary is printed there.

Giocuqet is bad or corrupted blood, with Nigotta chi as its Japanese explanation. The final r before the hyphen is weak but consistent with cor-rupto on the following row; the historical medical description is not updated into a diagnosis.

runs.text: rupto como o que deitão as molheres depois de

lines.note: Completes corrupto and compares it with blood discharged after childbirth. The scan supports rupto, uninterrupted como, and depois, correcting OCR rupio, co mo and depou.
Completes depois de parir, after giving birth. This is the final body continuation; the separate Gio. below it is a catchword, not part of the medical gloss.
